newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Buddhist funeral for Australia assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: Buddhist funeral for Australia assisted suicide.

text.p: A Buddhist funeral service will be held on Friday for the first man to die under Australia's world-first voluntary euthanasia law.
But the funeral of Bob Dent, whose death has renewed international debate over mercy killings, has also sparked a fresh controversy over whether he can be cremated or will have to be buried.
Dent, terminally ill with prostate cancer, died on Sunday after a computer-delivered lethal injection at his home in this sleepy tropical city, capital of Australia's Northern Territory.
The 66-year-old former carpenter and pilot became a Buddhist after he was diagnosed with cancer five years ago, turning to meditation and traditional Chinese treatment, locals said.
But a fresh controversy has erupted over whether he can be cremated in line with his wishes. Documents for the cremation require a doctor to say if the person died naturally.
Dent's paperwork shows he died under the Territory's world-first assisted suicide law.
A local government source told Reuters it was unclear if this would prevent Dent being cremated.
"We don't know if he can be cremated, like he and his wife wanted, or if he'll have to be buried," the source said.
Three local councils in charge of the crematorium will consult local Buddhist leaders to decide if Dent can be cremated. Dent's widow, Judy, was not available for comment.

His death has sparked a bitter and emotional debate, with opponents warning of legalised murder and moral decay and supporters describing assisted suicide as "beautiful" and a victory for personal choice.
Dent, in an emotional open letter written on the eve of his death, pleaded with Australia's national parliament not to overturn the law.

"What right has anyone because of their own religious faith, to which I don't subscribe, to demand that I behave according to their rules and endure unnecessary intractable pain," Dent wrote in an open letter penned on the eve of his death.

A backbencher in Prime Minister John Howard's conservative government has launched a private action in parliament, with Howard's support, which would see Canberra use its constitutional powers to wipe out the territory law.
The assisted suicide law has sparked widespread condemnation from Australia's political leaders, medical, church and aboriginal groups and the Vatican.
But opinion polls show overwhelming backing for the law among ordinary Australians, with some polls showing up to 80 percent support.
Dent's doctor, euthanasia crusader Philip Nitschke, told Reuters on Friday that Dent's death had paved the way for more assisted suicides.

Nitschke, who has already watched one patient die in agony while legal and political wrangles prevented use of the euthanasia law, said he had another five terminally-ill patients who wanted to die under the legislation.
The Territory's law, which took effect from July, allows dying people to kill themselves with a lethal injection or pills, if three doctors support their bid.
The euthanasia issue has split Australian public opinion.
The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper came out strongly against the euthanasia law in an editorial on Friday but its sister newspaper, The Age, in Melbourne voiced support.

"The first legally assisted suicide in Australia is a triumph of the dangerous belief that everything in life, even the moment of death, can be improved by suitable legislation," the Herald said under the headline "Mercy Death Splits Nation."
However, The Age's editorial supported the Territory's law and argued that federal parliament should not strike it down.

"...We believe that it is preferable to bring consensual mercy killing into the open under stringent conditions that hold those who exercise it accountable for their decisions," the newspaper said in an editorial headlined "Let the Quality of Mercy not be Restrained".
